newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Congress adjourns amid election hopes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Congress adjourns amid election hopes.

text.p: The U.S. Senate adjourned for the year on Thursday, preparing to end the 104th Congress and start the final push of an election campaign that both parties hope will give them control in the new session.

Virtually all members of the House of Representatives left town last weekend although the House has remained technically in session. It will formally quit on Friday, completing the earliest congressional adjournment in 20 years.

Republicans say they are confident that when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 7, they will still be in charge. Democrats have been predicting the Nov. 5 elections will put them in the majority, reversing the Republican takeover two years ago.
Analysts have said there is an outside chance of a change of power.

Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle predicted this week that the new Senate will have a 52-48 Democratic majority but Republican Leader Trent Lott said on Thursday he believed his party, now holding a 53-47 edge, would make a net gain of two or three seats.
Among the seats up for grabs are those occupied by 14 senators and 42 representatives who are retiring.
In its final day of business the Senate cleared two major bills for presidential signature.

It approved a measure authorising billions of dollars for the Federal Aviation Administration and airport safety after cutting off a filibuster led by Sen. Edward Kennedy, D-Massachusetts, over a provision he said would hamper efforts by Federal Express Corp truck drivers to become unionized.

The Senate also approved a scaled-down version of a bill to add or expand a number of national parks after Alaska Republican Frank Murkowski won agreement from the White House to keep timber from the Tongass National Forest flowing to two southeast Alaska sawmills for two years.
Also headed for the White House was a bill passed late on Wednesday that would make theft of trade secrets a crime and set prison penalties for foreign economic espionage.

Lott and Daschle made a traditional end-of-session telephone call informing the president that Congress had finished its work, although they later returned to the chamber to complete action on a flock of minor bills.

"You guys did such a great job. It's amazing how much was done here in the last few weeks. You should really be proud," replied Clinton, who won much of what he wanted in negotiations on a huge bill funding much of the government for the fiscal year that began on Tuesday.
